what_its_for: Haloperidol decanoate is used to treat schizophrenia and other conditions that cause confused thinking, hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there), and unusual behavior. It belongs to a group of medicines called antipsychotics. This long-acting injectable form helps keep your symptoms under control over a longer period of time without needing to take a pill every day.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) into a muscle, usually in your buttock. A healthcare provider such as a nurse or doctor will give you this injection in a clinic or medical office. You will NOT inject this medicine yourself at home. Each injection is usually given once every 4 weeks (once a month), but your doctor will decide the schedule that is right for you. Try to keep all of your injection appointments. If you need to reschedule, call your clinic as soon as possible.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition, your response to the medicine, and any other medications you take. Doses are measured in milligrams (mg). Common doses range from 10 mg to 200 mg or more per injection, given every 4 weeks. Never try to change your dose on your own. Always talk to your doctor before making any changes.
missed_dose: If you miss or are late for your scheduled injection appointment, call your doctor or clinic right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not wait until your next regular appointment. Missing injections can cause your symptoms to come back. Your doctor may adjust your dose or schedule after a missed injection.
storage: This medicine is stored and handled only by your healthcare provider or pharmacy. You do not need to store it at home. If for any reason you are given a supply to bring to another facility, keep it at room temperature (59°F to 77°F / 15°C to 25°C), away from light, heat, and moisture. Keep it out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while using this medicine, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness and cause serious side effects. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires you to be alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid getting up too quickly from sitting or lying down, as this medicine can cause your blood pressure to drop suddenly, making you feel dizzy or faint. Avoid overheating or becoming dehydrated, especially in hot weather or during exercise, as this medicine can affect your body's ability to cool itself. Tell your doctor about ALL other medications you take, including over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements, as many medicines can interact with haloperidol.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following: uncontrollable movements of your face, tongue, lips, arms, or legs (this could be a condition called tardive dyskinesia); muscle stiffness, high fever, sweating, or confusion (signs of a rare but serious condition called Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome or NMS); fast or irregular heartbeat, or fainting; difficulty breathing or swallowing; severe dizziness; signs of low white blood cell count such as fever, chills, or sore throat; thoughts of harming yourself; seizures; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); or any new or worsening symptoms that worry you. Also call your doctor if you notice unusual, repetitive movements of your mouth or body that you cannot control.
when_it_works: Haloperidol decanoate does not work immediately. After your first injection, it may take several days to a few weeks before you start to notice improvement in your symptoms. The medicine builds up in your body slowly and reaches steady levels over several weeks. Many people notice the best results after receiving a few regular injections. Do not stop your injections even if you feel better, because stopping suddenly can cause your symptoms to come back.
special_populations: Older adults: Older people, especially those with dementia, may be more sensitive to the side effects of this medicine, including falls, dizziness, and confusion. Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis should NOT use this medicine, as it can increase the risk of death. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Babies born to mothers who take antipsychotic medicines in the third trimester may have muscle stiffness or withdrawal symptoms after birth. Breastfeeding: This medicine may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: This long-acting injectable form is generally not used in children. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted.
